protagonist.name: Maya
protagonist.description: a young architect with short black hair, wearing a grey turtleneck and safety glasses

video_prompts.prompt: Scene: A minimalist, dark studio lit by a central hologram. Maya, a young architect with short black hair, wearing a grey turtleneck and safety glasses, stands before a large, glowing wireframe model of a bridge truss. She touches a control panel, and one angle of a triangular support beam begins to increase. As the angle widens, the vertical beam (opposite side) visibly lengthens while the horizontal beam (adjacent side) shortens to maintain connection. Glowing measurement lines update in real-time, showing the direct relationship between the angle and the side lengths. The camera slowly dollies in towards the changing angle. Final frame: A close-up on the triangle, with the angle and all three sides highlighted.

Scene: Eye-level shot in a futuristic workshop. Maya, a young architect with short black hair, wearing a grey turtleneck and safety glasses, manipulates a holographic right-angled triangle. She isolates the angle 'A'. The side opposite angle A glows bright magenta, detaches, and floats upwards. The hypotenuse glows cyan and moves below it, forming a division line. The text 'Opposite' and 'Hypotenuse' materializes next to the corresponding sides. The complete formula 'Sin A = Opposite / Hypotenuse' assembles on screen. The camera cranes up to an overhead view, showing the constructed formula next to the original triangle. Final frame: Top-down view of the triangle and the fully formed, glowing Sine formula.

Scene: A medium shot in the same workshop setting. Maya, a young architect with short black hair, wearing a grey turtleneck and safety glasses, resets the hologram. This time, she selects the side adjacent to angle 'A', which glows a vibrant orange. The adjacent side detaches and moves to the numerator position. The hypotenuse, still glowing cyan, detaches and slides into the denominator position below the orange side. The labels 'Adjacent' and 'Hypotenuse' appear. The camera orbits 90 degrees around the action as the formula 'Cos A = Adjacent / Hypotenuse' is constructed. Final frame: A side view of the completed Cosine formula floating beside the triangle.

Scene: A low-angle shot looking up at the hologram. Maya, a young architect with short black hair, wearing a grey turtleneck and safety glasses, gestures again. The magenta 'Opposite' side and the orange 'Adjacent' side both glow intensely. They simultaneously detach from the triangle, with the hypotenuse fading to a dim wireframe. The magenta side takes the numerator position while the orange side takes the denominator position. The text 'Tan A = Opposite / Adjacent' assembles piece by piece. The camera pushes in slowly towards the newly formed fraction. Final frame: A direct, centered shot of the glowing Tangent formula, clear and legible.

Scene: A wide shot showing two separate holographic right triangles, ABC and PQR, floating side-by-side. Maya, a young architect with short black hair, wearing a grey turtleneck and safety glasses, observes them. The ratio for 'sin B' is calculated on the first triangle, glowing and displaying a value. Then, the ratio for 'sin Q' is calculated on the second, displaying the exact same value. The triangles then animate, with triangle PQR scaling up and rotating until it perfectly superimposes over triangle ABC. The angles B and Q flash with a bright white light, showing they are identical. The camera zooms into the overlapping angles. Final frame: A close-up of the two perfectly aligned triangles, with angle B and Q merged into one.

narration.full_text: Welcome to our recap of the Introduction to Trigonometry. In this chapter, we explored the fundamental relationships between the sides and angles of right-angled triangles. We started by defining trigonometry as the study of these very relationships, which are crucial for understanding many areas of mathematics and science. We then delved into the core concepts: the six trigonometric ratios. Remember, these ratios are sine, cosine, tangent, cosecant, secant, and cotangent. Each ratio expresses a specific relationship between the lengths of the sides of a right-angled triangle relative to one of its acute angles. For instance, the sine of an angle is the ratio of the length of the opposite side to the length of the hypotenuse. We also learned how to apply the Pythagorean theorem in conjunction with these ratios to find unknown side lengths or to determine all trigonometric ratios when one is given. For example, if you know the tangent of an angle, you can construct a right triangle and use Pythagoras to find the hypotenuse, allowing you to calculate all other ratios. Finally, we examined important properties and identities, such as proving that if the sines of two acute angles are equal, then the angles themselves must be equal. This demonstrated how these ratios can be used in proofs and problem-solving. Understanding these concepts forms a strong foundation for more advanced topics in trigonometry. Keep practicing these definitions and examples to solidify your knowledge!
